title: GRAVL-BERT: Graphical Visual-Linguistic Representations for Multimodal Coreference Resolution
research_question: Can multimodal coreference resolution in situated dialogue be improved by jointly encoding dialogue, candidate-object appearance, scene-graph spatial relationships, object metadata, conversational recency, and local environmental context?
methodology: GRAVL-BERT extends VL-BERT with a graph-convolutional representation of objects and their spatial relationships in a scene. Its inputs combine dialogue text, object metadata, reference-distance features, full-scene and candidate-region visual features, neighboring-object information, generated environmental captions, segment information, and positional signals. The model is trained for binary candidate-object classification on SIMMC 2.0, with dialogue-domain pretraining and negative downsampling, and predicts referred objects by thresholding candidate scores. Component ablations and error-category analyses measure the contribution of graph, recency, neighboring, and caption features.

key_findings.finding: GRAVL-BERT reaches approximately 0.78 F1 on SIMMC 2.0 and is reported as the strongest system among the compared challenge submissions.
Dialogue-domain pretraining alone markedly improves VL-BERT over the vanilla configuration, raising the reported development F1 from roughly 0.47 to roughly 0.68.
Adding graph-convolutional scene relationships raises development F1 further, showing that explicit spatial structure contributes useful grounding information.
Reference distance produces one of the largest incremental gains in the ablation sequence, supporting the usefulness of conversational recency for resolving referring expressions.
Neighbor features and generated environmental captions provide additional smaller improvements after graph and reference-distance features are included.

The paper's error analysis reports large reductions across spatial, dialogue-history, metadata, pure-visual, and non-target-object error categories relative to the dialogue-pretrained VL-BERT baseline.
The model grounds dialogue references to candidate scene objects but does not establish persistent object identity across revised versions of a document or interface.

limitations: Evaluation is limited to SIMMC 2.0's simulated fashion and furniture shopping environments, so behavior on natural documents, workbooks, emails, or production user interfaces is not established.

Dialogue context is restricted to three preceding turns because of transformer input-length constraints and an assumption that recent context is most relevant, limiting long-range reference resolution.
Environmental captions are generated by an additional vision-language pipeline and heuristically incorporated, creating another potential source of error.
The approach assumes a provided candidate-object inventory and scene relationships rather than evaluating end-to-end detection and relation extraction from unconstrained real images.
Each candidate object is scored as a binary decision with a fixed threshold, so performance depends on candidate generation and calibration.
The model resolves object coreference within a scene/dialogue context rather than lineage across artifact revisions.
It does not represent document-specific hierarchical coordinates such as version-page-region, workbook-sheet-row-column-cell, or attachment-version identifiers.
raw_claims: GRAVL-BERT combines visual-linguistic transformer representations with a graph representation of spatial relationships among scene objects.
The model uses SIMMC 2.0, a dataset of roughly eleven thousand task-oriented dialogues situated in virtual fashion and furniture environments.
Its graph encodes spatial relations such as left, right, above, below, and containment among candidate objects.
Reference distance represents how many dialogue turns have elapsed since the candidate object was most recently mentioned by the system.
Training uses dialogue-domain masked-language-model pretraining before multimodal coreference fine-tuning.
The vanilla VL-BERT baseline has development F1 around 0.47, while dialogue pretraining raises it to about 0.68.
Adding the graph component raises F1 to about 0.72, and adding reference distance raises it to about 0.77.
Neighboring-object features and generated captions provide further smaller gains, producing development F1 of about 0.783.
The reported test F1 is approximately 0.78 and the paper reports first place among the compared SIMMC 2.0 challenge systems.
The implementation is publicly released and the repository provides instructions for obtaining the SIMMC 2.0 data.
